title: Approximately Decoding the Colour Code
abstract: Recently we showed that minimum weight decoding in the (6.6.6 planar) colour code is NP-hard. However, it remained an open question as to whether it was possible to approximate the minimum weight decoding arbitrarily closely in polynomial time. In this paper we prove that it is possible: for any $\varepsilon>0$ there is an polynomial time algorithm that, given a syndrome, can find an error-set generating that syndrome whose weight is at most $1+\varepsilon$ times the weight of the minimum weight decoding. As a consequence we see that, for any $\varepsilon>0$, there is a polynomial time algorithm that can correct all errors of weight up to $(1-\varepsilon)d/2$ in the distance $d$ colour code (so almost up to the theoretical $d/2$ limit).   The polynomial we give is impractically large, but it does open the door for sensible polynomial time algorithms that approximate minimum weight decoding and, in particular, shows that approximate decoding is not NP-hard.
summary: This paper proves that one can find an error-set in the colour code whose weight approximates the true minimum weight decoding within an arbitrary factor $(1+\epsilon)$ using only polynomial time. This result demonstrates that approximate quantum decoding is computationally feasible, despite the underlying exact problem being NP-hard.
main_problem: The core problem is determining whether approximate minimum weight decoding for quantum error-correcting codes, specifically the colour code, can be achieved in polynomial time.
main_result: The authors prove that it is possible to find an error-set whose weight is within $(1+\epsilon)$ of the true minimum weight decoding in polynomial time, showing approximate decoding is not NP-hard.
method: The approach adapts techniques from solving Euclidean optimization problems (like Arora's work), using dynamic programming and imposing structural constraints (portal respecting) to reduce the problem complexity iteratively.
model_or_system: The system modeled is the colour code, defined on an infinite hexagonal lattice or a finite region thereof. It is used as a quantum error-correcting code for detecting errors (X-errors) that generate a measurable syndrome.
key_observables: Syndrome ($S$), minimum weight decoding ($	ext{OPT}$), and the resulting approximate error-set weight $|E|$.
important_parameters: Approximation factor $\epsilon$, code distance $d$, lattice size parameters $L$ and $M$.
main_assumptions: The initial polynomial algorithm derived is noted to be impractically large in its complexity, requiring significant theoretical leaps for practical implementation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the colour code structure on lattices (hexagonal/triangular), how errors trigger checks based on location (bulk/boundary), and geometric decompositions using rhombuses or hexagons to constrain error sets.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first tackling the general approximation problem, then applying techniques involving lattice decomposition (rhombus tiling) and imposing structural constraints ('portal respecting') via dynamic programming. Finally, it refines this process for specific bounded regions of the code.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the computational complexity limits of quantum error correction, providing a theoretical breakthrough by showing that approximate decoding is tractable even when exact decoding is NP-hard.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The colour code and its error model. (a) The 6.6.6 colour code (with boundary). There are data qubits on the vertices of a hexagonal lattice and the checks are the coloured faces. An X-error on a bulk data qubit (the yellow star in the middle of the picture) triggers the three Z-checks shown ringed in black. However, an X-error on a qubit lying on a boundary, only triggers the two checks (faces) containing it (for example the yellow star on the middle right boundary); and if the error occurs it at a corner, it only triggers the single check that it is contained in (the yellow star in the bottom right). (b) The dual lattice of the colour code shown in (a). In this figure the nodes...
Figure 2: (a) A rhombus consisting of sixteen tiles. (b) Two adjacent tiles with six errors joining them: one of each colour-orientation.

Figure 3: (a) Given an error f (the red triangle) look in the nearest portal tile (the rhombus shown) and pick the error p with the same colour-orientation (the green triangle) in the nearest portal tile (the tile shown). (b) We can join the red error to the green error by two ‘paths’ as shown: the set of all the shown errors has no syndrome, so the syndrome of the combined yellow and green errors (together these form Ef) is the same as the syndrome of the red error.

Figure 4: The distance 11 reduced colour code – the triangular region T shows the embedding of the bounded colour code. We have omitted the checks on the boundary of the triangle as they are not enforced in the reduced colour code. The two key points of the reduced code are that it is infinite so we can apply the modifications we used in Section 5, and if an error set is entirely inside T then its syndrome is identical in the bounded colour code and the reduced colour code.

Figure 5: The four steps in the post-processing described in Lemma 12; working clockwise from the top left: (a) we start with the original error-set. Top right (b): we have the error-set viewed as edges; note one edge (shown as two arcs) is actually a double edge so cancels with itself. Then bottom right (d) we have the projected edge error-set, and then bottom left (c) the actual post-processed error-set. We see that the syndrome of the two sets is the same except for the third row (nodes circled in red).
